title: Bubble Remobilization and Flow Regime Transitions in Non‐Darcy Gas–Liquid Flow Through Heterogeneous Porous Media
content:
Abstract

The transition from Darcy to non-Darcy flow in gas-liquid systems within heterogeneous porous media remains poorly understood, limiting predictive capabilities for processes such as geological carbon storage and groundwater remediation. This study integrates microfluidic experiments with theoretical analysis to elucidate how pore-scale bubble dynamics control macroscopic flow regimes. A critical capillary number (Ca), Ca crit ≈ 8.9 × 10−7, is identified to demarcate the transition between flow regimes. Below Ca crit, the flow obeys Darcy's law, characterized by a linear pressure gradient and continuous gas pathways. Above Ca crit, non-Darcy behavior emerges, characterized by a power-law relationship between pressure gradient and capillary number (exponent ≈ 0.5), driven by selective gas breakup, dynamic bubble remobilization, and intermittent flow. Pore structure heterogeneity affects bubble morphology: smaller bubbles migrate in near-spherical shapes, whereas larger bubbles are immobilized within pores of low shape factor. Increasing capillary number enhances bubble breakup, broadening the bubble-size distribution and intensifying flow intermittency. Optimal gas trapping occurs at low Ca and a gas fractional flow of 0.8. Based on these observations, we develop a pore-scale non-Darcy two-phase flow model that links bubble morphology to hydraulic resistance. This work establishes a mechanistic bridge between pore-scale interfacial processes and macro-scale non-Darcy flow, offering new insights for predicting and controlling multiphase transport in subsurface environments.
